title: Otto Lilienthal, the Glider King
summary: A German engineer named Otto Lilienthal watched storks, built bat-shaped wings and jumped off hills to glide through the air, more than 2,000 times! Photos of him flying amazed the whole world. Other brave pioneers, like Percy Pilcher in Britain and Octave Chanute in America, joined the race to fly.

sections.heading: Two Boys Who Watched the Storks
paragraphs: Picture a small town on the flat, marshy plains of northern Germany in the 1850s. The town is called Anklam, in a region then known as Pomerania, part of the Kingdom of Prussia. Every spring, big white storks with long red legs and black-tipped wings come flapping back from Africa to build huge, messy nests on the rooftops and chimneys. Two brothers stand in a meadow, heads tipped back, watching the storks glide in great slow circles without seeming to move their wings at all. How do they do that? the boys wonder. And could a person do it too?

The older boy was Karl Wilhelm Otto Lilienthal, born in Anklam on 23 May 1848. His younger brother Gustav was born the following year, in 1849. The family was not rich, and their father died when the boys were still young, but their mother encouraged their curiosity. Otto and Gustav studied the birds around them, especially storks, which are large, heavy birds that still manage to float effortlessly on the wind. A heavy bird that can glide, the brothers reasoned, was proof that air could hold up something big.

Like many dreamers before them, the boys first tried the obvious thing. They built wings that strapped onto their arms and ran about trying to flap their way into the sky. It did not work. As you saw in Part 2, the Italian scientist Giovanni Borelli had already explained in 1680 that human muscles are far too weak to flap wings like a bird. But the failure did not stop Otto. It just made him want to understand the problem properly.

At school in Anklam, from 1856 to 1864, Otto had a teacher who mattered: the astronomer Gustav Spörer, who taught him mathematics and also the study of birds. Then Otto trained to become an engineer, first at a regional technical school in Potsdam, then with a practical internship at the Schwartzkopff machine-building company in Berlin, and finally at the Royal Technical Academy in Berlin from 1867 to 1870. He was a strong student with a talent for designing machines.

His studies were interrupted by war. In 1870 and 1871, during the Franco-Prussian War, Otto served for a year as a soldier during the siege of Paris. Afterwards he returned to Berlin and worked as a design engineer for machine factories. In 1877 he received his first patent, for a machine used in mining. Over his life he would earn 25 patents, four of them for flying inventions.

In 1883 Otto started his own company in Berlin, making steam boilers and small steam engines. He designed a small engine with tubular boilers that he believed was much safer than other engines of the time, which sometimes exploded. The factory earned the money that paid for his flying experiments. Otto was also unusually kind as a boss for his era: in 1890 he began sharing 25 percent of the factory's profits with his workers, and he supported a people's theatre in Berlin so that ordinary families could enjoy plays. He and Gustav even invented a set of children's stone building blocks, called Anchor Stone Blocks, which later became famous in Germany.

Otto married Agnes Fischer in 1878, and they had four children. He was a busy factory owner, father and inventor. Yet the question from the stork meadow never left him. Gustav had spent years living in Australia, and when he returned to Germany in the mid-1880s, the two brothers took up their old dream together, this time as grown-up engineers.

sections.heading: A Book About How Birds Fly
paragraphs: Before Otto ever left the ground, he spent years measuring. Starting around 1867, the brothers built test equipment to find out exactly how much force the air pushes on wings of different shapes. One of their devices was a whirling arm, similar to the one Sir George Cayley used (you met him in Part 3): a long arm that spun around a central post, carrying a small test wing through the air so its push could be measured. They tested flat plates and curved plates, tilted at different angles, and wrote down the numbers.

Their most important discovery was this: a wing that is gently curved, arching upward like the wing of a stork, makes far more lift than a flat board. This curve is called camber. Birds have it, and Otto realised it was no accident. A curved wing turns the air flowing past it downward more smoothly and efficiently, and in return the air pushes the wing up. Many earlier experimenters had used flat surfaces in their calculations. Otto proved with real measurements that curved was better.

In 1889 he published everything in a book. Its German title was Der Vogelflug als Grundlage der Fliegekunst, which means Birdflight as the Basis of Aviation. (The English translation did not appear until 1911, so English-speaking inventors at first learned about his work through articles and summaries.) The book was packed with drawings of bird wings, careful measurements and tables of numbers showing how much lift and drag a curved wing made at each angle.

Otto also invented a clever way to draw this information as a single curved graph, which engineers today call a polar diagram. On it, you can see at a glance how lift and drag change together as the angle of the wing changes. Aircraft designers still use this kind of diagram more than a century later. Wilbur Wright later wrote that nobody did as much as Lilienthal to convince the world of the advantages of curved wing surfaces.

The book was not perfect. Otto still believed that the best long-term answer might be flapping wings, like a bird's, and he spent some of his later years building flapping-wing machines that never worked well. And, as you will see in Part 6 and Part 7, his famous tables of numbers would later cause trouble for two brothers in America. But in 1889 the book was a giant step: it treated flight as a science, built on measurements instead of guesses.

There was one more lesson in the book, and it was perhaps the most important. Otto believed you could not learn to fly just by doing sums at a desk. You had to go out into the real wind and practise, over and over, the way a young bird practises. Thinking about flying, he argued, was not the same as flying. So, at around the age of 43, the factory owner from Berlin decided to become a pilot.

sections.heading: Leaping From the Hills
paragraphs: In the spring of 1891, Otto took his first proper glider to a sloping sand pit near the villages of Derwitz and Krielow, west of Potsdam. His glider looked like a pair of giant bat wings. Its frame was made of light willow rods, covered with tightly stretched cotton cloth, with a curved shape copied from the birds he had studied for so long. There was no seat, no cockpit and no engine. Otto simply stood inside an opening in the middle of the wings, gripped the frame and rested his forearms on padded supports, so that he hung beneath the glider with his legs dangling.

To launch, he ran down the slope into the wind until the air under the wings lifted him. That first year his hops were short, about 25 metres. But they were real glides: the air, not his legs, was holding him up. Every flight taught him something, and each winter he improved his designs.

How did he steer? This is the key to Lilienthal's method. His gliders had a fixed tail to keep them pointing into the wind, but no moving controls at all. Instead, Otto steered by swinging his body. If the nose started to rise too high, he threw his legs forward to move his weight toward the front, which tipped the nose down. If one wing dropped, he swung his hips and legs toward the other side to level it. Modern hang-glider pilots still use this idea of weight-shifting, though today's gliders are much bigger and easier to handle.

Otto needed safe places to practise near home. In 1892 he built a shed with a tower on a hill called the Maihöhe in Steglitz, Berlin, giving him a jump-off point about 10 metres high. Then, around 1893 to 1894, he did something remarkable: he had an artificial hill built near his home in Lichterfelde, a suburb of Berlin. It was a cone of earth about 15 metres high, with a shed for his gliders tucked inside the top. Because it was round, he could always launch straight into the wind, whichever direction it blew. Berliners called it the Fliegeberg, the Flying Hill. It still stands today, now a memorial in a park.

For longer flights, Otto travelled northwest of Berlin to a range of bare, grassy hills near the town of Rhinow. From 1893 he flew from a hill called the Hauptmannsberg there, and from 1896 also from the Gollenberg near the village of Stölln. On these higher slopes, with steady winds, his glides grew much longer. Some stretched to about 250 metres, a distance nobody else had come close to matching while he was alive.

Imagine being one of the farm children of Rhinow on a summer Sunday. Up on the hilltop stands a bearded man in a jacket and knickerbocker trousers, holding a huge pale wing above his head. He runs a few steps, leaps, and suddenly he is floating out over the slope, legs swinging, the cloth humming in the wind. A few seconds later, he lands softly in the grass far below, and a helper starts carrying the glider back up the hill so he can do it all again.

sections.heading: Two Thousand Glides and the Photos That Amazed the World
paragraphs: Between 1891 and 1896, Otto Lilienthal made more than 2,000 glides. Most lasted only a few seconds, and if you added up all his time in the air it came to only about five hours. That might not sound like much. But no human being before him had ever flown so often, so deliberately, and come back to try again. He was not a lucky tower jumper. He was a test pilot, gathering experience flight by flight.

He also kept inventing. He built about a dozen different single-wing (monoplane) gliders, two biplane gliders with one wing stacked above another, and several flapping-wing machines. In 1894 he began producing one design, which he called the Normalsegelapparat, meaning the standard sailing machine, and selling copies to other people. Its wings spanned about 6.7 metres and the whole glider weighed only about 20 kilograms, light enough for one person to carry. At least nine were sold. Because of this, the Otto Lilienthal Museum in Anklam calls it the world's first production aircraft: the first flying machine made in a series and sold to customers. Original Lilienthal gliders or pieces of them survive today in museums in London, Moscow, Munich and Washington.

What really made Lilienthal famous, though, was photography. Cameras in the 1890s were getting faster, and photographers came to the hills to try to capture him in the air. One of them was Ottomar Anschütz, a German pioneer of high-speed photography. Another was the American physicist Robert Williams Wood. At least 145 photographs of Lilienthal's flights are known. Sadly, the original glass negatives were destroyed during World War II, but prints had already travelled the world.

Think about how startling those pictures were. For thousands of years people had drawn and painted imaginary flying humans. Now magazines and newspapers in Germany, Britain, France, Russia and the United States printed real photographs of a real man soaring through the sky on wings he had built himself. You could see his legs hanging down, the shape of the wings, the hill below. Here at last was proof that a human could fly, at least in a glider.

Visitors came to see him for themselves. Among them were Samuel Langley, the American scientist whose steam-powered models you met in Part 4, and the Russian scientist Nikolai Zhukovsky, who later became one of the founders of Russian aeronautics and took a Lilienthal glider back to Moscow. A young British engineer named Percy Pilcher came too. Otto also wrote letters to experimenters around the world, including Octave Chanute in Chicago. He wrote articles for German science magazines, explaining what he had learned so that others could build on it.

Lilienthal knew that gliding was only the first step. His plan was to master control in the air first, and only then add an engine. He even began experimenting with a small engine using carbonic acid gas to flap the tips of a wing. But first, he believed, a pilot had to become truly at home in the wind.

sections.heading: The Last Flight
paragraphs: Sunday, 9 August 1896, was a bright summer day at the Gollenberg near Stölln. Otto was flying his standard glider. He had already made three flights that day. On the fourth, something went wrong. Partway through the glide, the glider pitched its nose up sharply. The Lilienthal Museum describes him being caught by a sudden pocket of rising warm air. The wing tilted too steeply against the airflow and stalled.

A stall, remember, has nothing to do with an engine (gliders do not even have one). It means the wing is meeting the air at too steep an angle, so the smooth airflow over the top breaks away and the lift suddenly collapses. The glider dropped. Otto threw his weight forward to bring the nose down, but swinging his body could only move the glider's balance a small amount, and it was not enough. From a height of about 15 metres, he fell to the ground.

He was badly hurt. A bone in his neck, the third cervical vertebra, was broken. He was carried from the hill and then taken to Berlin, to the clinic of the famous surgeon Ernst von Bergmann. But doctors could not save him. Otto Lilienthal died on 10 August 1896, the day after his fall. He was 48 years old.

People often repeat his supposed last words, Opfer müssen gebracht werden, meaning Sacrifices must be made. Those words are even carved on his gravestone. But historians are not sure he ever said them; the director of the Otto Lilienthal Museum has doubted it. So it is best to treat the famous phrase as a story rather than a proven fact.

What his death did prove was something important about flying. Weight-shifting worked well enough for an expert in gentle conditions, but in a sudden gust it was too weak. A pilot needed a better way to control a flying machine, one that did not depend on how far he could swing his legs. Gustav Lilienthal carried on with aviation work for decades, but Otto's death shocked experimenters everywhere. The question of control would become the central puzzle of the next few years.

sections.heading: Percy Pilcher, Britain's Flying Hawk
paragraphs: One of the people most inspired by Lilienthal was Percy Sinclair Pilcher. He was born in Bath, England, on 16 January 1867. As a boy of 13 he joined the Royal Navy as a cadet and served for seven years, then trained as an engineer at a shipbuilding company in Govan, Glasgow. From 1891 he worked as an assistant lecturer in engineering at the University of Glasgow.

In 1895 Pilcher built his first hang glider, which he called the Bat. Later that year he travelled to Germany to meet Otto Lilienthal himself and talk about gliding. What he learned helped him design two more gliders, the Beetle and the Gull. Then he built his best machine, the Hawk, based closely on Lilienthal's ideas but with a clever addition: wheels underneath, so it could roll across the ground.

Pilcher also found a new way to get into the air. Britain has fewer big sandy hills than the Rhinow area, so he often had his gliders towed into the wind by a line pulled by men or horses, a bit like launching a kite. In 1897, on the grounds of Stanford Hall, a country house in Leicestershire, the Hawk glided about 250 metres, a record for that time. His sister Ella helped him, sewing the cloth for the wings and assisting with test flights.

Pilcher wanted to go further than Lilienthal had. He designed a powered triplane, with three wings stacked one above another, meant to carry a small engine of about 4 horsepower. To build an engine he went into partnership with a motor engineer, Walter Gordon Wilson. The project cost a great deal of money, and Pilcher fell into debt. He needed wealthy sponsors.

On 30 September 1899 he invited important guests to Stanford Hall to watch a demonstration. But a few days earlier, the triplane's engine crankshaft had broken. Not wanting to disappoint his visitors, Pilcher decided to fly the Hawk glider instead. It had been raining, and the wet canvas wings had shrunk as they soaked up water, putting extra strain on the bamboo frame. While he was being towed into the air, the tail snapped. The Hawk fell from about 10 metres. Percy Pilcher died on 2 October 1899 without waking up. He was 32.

His triplane was never flown in public. More than a century later, in 2003, engineers at Cranfield University in England built a replica for a BBC television programme and found the design was more or less workable: their copy made a steady flight of 1 minute 25 seconds in calm air. Nobody can say for certain what would have happened if Pilcher had lived. His restored Hawk glider is displayed today at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh.

sections.heading: Octave Chanute, the Great Sharer
paragraphs: Across the Atlantic, a very different flying pioneer was at work. Octave Chanute was born in Paris on 18 February 1832, and his family moved to the United States when he was a small boy. He became one of America's leading civil engineers, the kind of person who designs bridges, railways and big structures. He helped design the Hannibal Bridge, opened in 1869, the first bridge to cross the Missouri River at Kansas City. He planned the vast stockyards of Chicago and Kansas City, and he developed a way of soaking railway sleepers (the wooden beams under the tracks) in chemicals so they would not rot. From 1873 to 1883 he was chief engineer of the Erie Railway.

When Chanute grew older and wealthier, he turned his practical mind to flight. He did something that sounds simple but was enormously valuable: he collected everything. He read reports, papers and letters from experimenters all over the world, from Cayley to Lilienthal, and wrote clear summaries of what each person had tried and what had happened. These appeared first as a series of articles from 1891 to 1893, and then, in 1894, as a book called Progress in Flying Machines. It was the most complete survey of attempts to build fixed-wing flying machines that had ever been published. In 1893 he also helped organise an international conference on aerial navigation at the World's Fair in Chicago.

Chanute was too old to be a daring pilot himself, but he wanted to test ideas in the real wind. In the summer of 1896, at the age of 64, he took a team to the sand dunes along the southern shore of Lake Michigan, near Miller Beach, Indiana. His helpers included the engineer Augustus Herring and a carpenter named William Avery. The dunes were perfect: soft sand to land on, steady winds blowing in off the lake, and no trees in the way.

The team tested several hang gliders. One had many small wings arranged in layers that could swing back slightly in a gust, and an early version had twelve wings. But their most successful glider was a two-surface machine: a biplane, with one long wing above another. Chanute braced the two wings together with upright posts and crossed wires, using a pattern called the Pratt truss that he knew from building railway bridges. This made the wings very strong and stiff without being heavy. Herring and Avery made many glides with it, the longest reported at roughly 100 metres, and steered it by shifting their weight, as Lilienthal had.

That strong, wire-braced biplane design turned out to be one of the most important ideas in early aviation. The Wright brothers later based the structure of their own kites, gliders and first airplane on Chanute's double-decker plan.

Above all, Chanute believed in sharing. He wrote hundreds of letters to experimenters in many countries, answered their questions, introduced them to one another, and passed on the latest results. In 1897 he helped bring Lilienthal's table of measurements for curved wings to English-speaking readers. In a time without the internet, Chanute was like a one-man information network for everyone trying to fly.

sections.heading: News Travels to Dayton
paragraphs: By the end of the 1890s, the picture looked both exciting and frightening. Lilienthal had shown that a person could glide again and again, and he had given the world measurements, photographs and a proven wing shape. Chanute had shown that a strong biplane glider was possible and had gathered all the world's flying knowledge in one book. Pilcher had been preparing to add an engine. Yet two of the boldest pilots, Lilienthal in 1896 and Pilcher in 1899, had died because their gliders could not be controlled well enough when something went wrong.

Meanwhile, in August 1896, newspapers around the world carried the sad news that the German Glider King had fallen to his death. In the city of Dayton, Ohio, the story reached two brothers who ran a small bicycle shop. They had been fascinated by flying since they were boys. Wilbur Wright later called Lilienthal 'without question the greatest of the precursors', meaning the greatest of the people who came before them. Lilienthal's death did not frighten the brothers away. It made them think hard about the one problem that had killed him: control. Their names were Wilbur and Orville Wright, and Part 6 tells their story.

deepDive: Lilienthal's lasting scientific gift was data. With his brother Gustav he measured the forces on curved and flat test surfaces at many angles, and in 1889 published the results as tables and as a 'polar diagram', a single curve plotting lift against drag as the angle of attack changes. Engineers still use polars today to choose wing shapes. His key finding, that a gently cambered surface produces much more lift for its drag than a flat plate, overturned the flat-plate assumptions that many earlier calculators had used. But his numbers came with hidden conditions. They described one particular wing curve, measured on a whirling arm and in natural wind, and they were usually applied together with an older multiplier for air pressure, the 'Smeaton coefficient', which turned out to be too high. When Chanute published Lilienthal's table in English in 1897, many experimenters, including the Wrights, used it as their starting point. The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum explains that the Wrights' early gliders underperformed predictions based partly on a misreading of that table, which pushed them to gather their own data. Historians also debate the limits of Lilienthal's control method. A hang-glider pilot steers by moving the combined centre of gravity of pilot and glider, but on a glider spanning about 6.7 metres the pilot can shift that centre only a few centimetres. In calm air this is enough; in a sudden gust or thermal it may not be. His fatal stall in 1896 showed this weakness, and it is one reason the Wrights later insisted on movable control surfaces instead. Another debate is about what might have happened had he lived. Lilienthal was working on engines, and Pilcher's triplane was nearly ready in 1899; a 2003 Cranfield University replica of Pilcher's design flew for 85 seconds in calm air. Yet most historians caution that a workable machine is not the same as a controllable one, and that neither man had solved roll control in a way that would scale up. Finally, Lilienthal's 'over 2,000 flights' deserve context: each was short, the total airtime was only about five hours, and yet that was far more real flying experience than anyone else on Earth had at the time.
funFact: Otto Lilienthal had a cone-shaped hill about 15 metres high built near his home in Berlin just so he could launch his gliders into the wind from any direction, and it still stands today.
